AM7I-10.note: Genuinely hard: the whole item is the fact that rates do not average. 12.5 is the arithmetic mean of 15 and 10 and will take most of the field. One of the best items in the batch.

AM7I-12.note: 40 = 18/45, 30 = red share. Building the whole first is the only extra step.

But the distractors are thin: 60, 66 and 84 have no clean wrong derivation I can find, so the item is easier than it should be by elimination.

AM7I-15.note: 188 = applying the coupon first (235 x 0.8), 200 = stopping early. Sequential rather than interacting, so medium.

AM7I-17.note: 15 = 3 x 5, 25 = 5^2. Surface area (150) is not offered, which is the distractor I would have expected.

AM7I-18.note: 6 (the number of student tickets) is exactly the right trap for a stem that asks for dollars.

AM7I-19.note: A rate that changes partway, but the two phases never interact - it is three independent steps in the order the stem gives them. 58 (total run time) and 70 (whole tank at the slow rate) are good. Medium on a real form.

AM7I-20.note: 48 = stopping at tablespoons, which is the whole point of the second conversion.

AM7I-21.note: Hard and clean: successive percents run backwards, and 969 (= 1020 x 0.95, the 'net 5% change' error) is a genuinely strong distractor.

AM7I-22.solved: Frequencies 2, 5, 6, 8 for 0, 1, 2, 3 siblings; total 21, so the median is the 11th value. Cumulative 2, 7, 13 - the 11th falls in the '2 siblings' column. Median = 2.
AM7I-22.note: TABLE CHECK: the table is internally consistent. 2+5+6+8 = 21, which matches the '21 students' in both the stem and the caption, and the sibling row (0,1,2,3) and student row (2,5,6,8) are aligned under the same four column rules. No disagreement. Distractor 1.95 is the mean (41/21 = 1.952) and 3 is the mode - both real. One weakness: n=21 is odd and the data are integers, so the median must be an integer; 1.5 and 1.95 are eliminable from the option set alone, without reading the table, leaving a 50/50 between 2 and 3.

AM7I-23.note: Hard at the low end. The interaction is real (recover x, then re-sort and notice x lands at the top so the middle is unchanged) and 22 - stopping at x - is the trap. But 16.5 is not a legal median of five numbers, so the field is narrowable to three without solving.

AM7I-24.note: 16.80 (overage only) and 111.80 (charging all 640 minutes) are both real errors.

AM7I-25.solved: 2 cm = 6 m, so 1 cm = 3 m. Garden is 21 m by 27 m; area = 567.
AM7I-25.note: Hard: linear scale versus area scale is a genuine second idea, and 126 (= 63 x 2, scaling the area by the linear factor) catches exactly the student who misses it. 63 = the drawing's own area.

AM7I-26.note: 4200 = 70 x 60 (dividing the perimeter by 4), 8400 = 70 x 120 (halving nothing). Routine two-step.

AM7I-27.note: 9.09 = dividing by the new wage is the standard percent-change error. The numbers are chosen so the correct division is exact, which makes it easier than it looks.

AM7I-28.note: 5.80 = the sum of the two known prices, 3.40 = echoing the mean. Same mean-to-total habit as 05, 13, 23.
